title: Luxor to Aswan: Train, Car, Cruise or the Temple Road?
excerpt: Luxor to Aswan and back: train, private car, Nile cruise from €500 or a guided Temple Road day via Esna, Edfu and Kom Ombo from €54, compared on time, cost and what you see.
body_html:
Prices, timetables and visiting details are a November 2026 snapshot. Check the linked official pages and your departure’s current inclusions and terms before booking.

The quick answer

Luxor and Aswan are about 215 to 245 km apart by road, roughly three hours by car on the direct road and about three and a half by train, and there are four ways to cover them, in either direction: the train (cheapest, sees nothing), a private car (flexible, no guide), a Nile cruise (four or five days, everything slowly) or the guided Temple Road, one day via the river temples of Esna, Edfu and Kom Ombo. Sawa lists three road days: Luxor to Aswan via Esna, Edfu and Kom Ombo (about 8 hours, from €67), a shorter Luxor to Aswan day via Edfu and Kom Ombo (about 6.5 hours, from €54), and Aswan to Luxor downriver via Kom Ombo, Edfu and Esna (about 8 hours, from €60), all per person, as listed in November 2026. If you have one day and want the temples, take the Temple Road.

Check current UK government travel advice for Egypt before making your arrangements; advice can change.

Between Luxor and Aswan lie three of the best temples on the Nile, Esna, Edfu and Kom Ombo, and four very different ways of dealing with the distance between the two cities. Most travellers rush it. This guide compares the four ways properly, in both directions, with the time, the cost and what each one actually shows you, so the leg between the two cities becomes part of the trip instead of dead time. It is written by the team behind Sawa Tours (sawa.tours), the Egypt shared-departure platform.

What is the best way to get between Luxor and Aswan?

The best way depends on one resource you cannot buy more of: days. Four options cover the distance, and each trades time against what you see.

The train is the cheapest and, on paper, the fastest, but it is pure transport: the river slides past a window and no temples are involved. A private car with a driver adds flexibility and stops, without guiding. The Nile cruise turns the journey into four or five days of slow sightseeing with meals and guiding included. And the Temple Road, a guided day via the river temples, compresses the cruise's temple stops into one day at a fixed per-person price.

Time-rich travellers take the cruise; point-to-point travellers on a budget take the train; and travellers with one day and a temple list take the Temple Road. The rest of this guide prices all four honestly.

How far is Luxor from Aswan?

Luxor and Aswan are about 215 km apart on the direct road (Rome2Rio puts it at 133 miles and just over three hours by car), or about 245 km if you follow the riverside route through Esna, Edfu and Kom Ombo, which is how the Earth Trekkers guide measures it. The rail line and the road both run along the Nile, and the river itself is the slower lane: cruise boats take days where the road takes hours.

The temples do not sit in either city. They sit on the corridor between them, which is the fact the whole comparison turns on. The road legs, per Earth Trekkers (updated December 2025), run Aswan to Kom Ombo about 47 km, Kom Ombo to Edfu about 70 km, Edfu to Esna about 64 km and Esna to Luxor about 64 km.

The four ways, side by side

Every option on one table. Train fares are the foreigner prices published by Seat 61 (page last updated 14 September 2026, checked 8 November 2026). Foreigners have paid separate dollar prices on Egyptian trains since December 2022. Sawa prices are per person, as listed in November 2026.

Option 1: the train, cheapest and you see nothing

The train is the budget answer. Trains between Luxor and Aswan take about three and a half hours. The range of fares is wide because it follows the class of train: roughly US$26 for a Russian-built third-class non-air-conditioned car, US$35 to US$40 on the VIP and Express services, and US$62 to US$77 on the Talgo (Seat 61).

There is a cheaper trick. Seat 61 lists US$10 for the Luxor to Aswan hop in seat mode on the sleeper trains 86 and 87. Whether seats are free on the day is for the sleeper operator, Abela, to say, so ask when you book.

Buying is not as simple as it looks. The Egyptian National Railways website and app sell Egyptian-price tickets to Egyptians only. Foreigners buy at the "Tourist tickets" window at Luxor and Aswan stations, or through agencies such as 12Go and Bookaway. What the train does not do is stop. Esna, Edfu and Kom Ombo are on the corridor the train ignores, and you arrive having seen the river through a window and nothing else. As transport between hotels it works; as sightseeing it is the empty option.

Option 2: a private car with driver, control without guiding

A private car with driver covers the direct road in about three hours, with the freedom to stop where you ask. Esna's temple sits in the town close to the route and Kom Ombo sits on the river bank beside it, so a car can tick off both with a little planning.

There is no guide included: the driver drives. The cost splits well across a group of three or four, which is where this option is at its best: families and photographers who have arranged their own guiding, or travellers who want a door-to-door day shaped entirely by them. Everyone else is paying private prices and still reading the temple signs alone.

Two practical points. Foreigners can hire a car and drive themselves, but Earth Trekkers advise against it, citing chaotic traffic, higher speeds on rural roads and language difficulties at the many police checkpoints, and recommend hiring a driver. And the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) warns against driving outside main cities and resorts at night, so plan to arrive before dark.

Option 3: the Nile cruise, the classic, priced in days

The Nile cruise is the journey as destination: four or five days on the water, the temples at the stops, full board on the boat, and the river doing the travelling. Sawa's shared cruise departures run it in both directions:

  • Nile Discovery, four days, Aswan to Luxor, from €500 per person, departing Wednesdays and Fridays. It includes a five-star cruiser with full board, a licensed Egyptologist guide, site tickets, a Luxor to Cairo flight and a Cairo dinner cruise.
  • Nile Majesty, five days, Luxor to Aswan, from €610 per person, departing Mondays and Saturdays. It includes a five-star cruiser with full board, a licensed guide, site tickets and a carriage ride.

On both, your group of up to 8 sails on a shared five-star ship and does the excursions together with its guide. Both list Edfu and Kom Ombo among their temples; Esna is not on either itinerary, which is one reason the road day still has its place. Packages take a 25% deposit at the GoAhead, the balance 14 days before, and need four travellers by 30 days before; see each package page for what it includes.

The honest cost is measured in days, not just money: the cruise asks for most of a week's itinerary. If you have the days, it is the richest version of this corridor. If you do not, the road is where your temples live.

Option 4: the Temple Road, the temples in one guided day

The Temple Road is the answer for travellers with one day and a temple list: a guided road day between the two cities with the river temples on the way. Sawa lists it three ways.

Luxor to Aswan via Esna, Edfu and Kom Ombo (departure page), about 8 hours, from €67 per person. As listed on 8 November 2026, the price covers a licensed guide, transport, hotel pickup in Luxor, drop-off in Aswan, lunch and the entrance tickets; gratuities are extra. The temples come in southbound order: Esna, then Edfu, then Kom Ombo.

Luxor to Aswan via Edfu and Kom Ombo (departure page), about 6.5 hours, from €54 per person. It skips Esna for a shorter day; check the departure page for what is included.

Aswan to Luxor downriver via Kom Ombo, Edfu and Esna (departure page), about 8 hours, from €60 per person. As listed on 8 November 2026, it includes a licensed guide, air-conditioned transport, Aswan hotel pickup, Luxor hotel drop-off and bottled water, and includes temple entrance tickets and lunch. The Kom Ombo Crocodile Museum ticket and gratuities are extras. Do not assume the two directions include the same things: read the page before you reserve.

All three are shared departures: travellers are pooled onto one date and the group never exceeds eight. The honest trade of the whole option: it is a long driving day stitched around temple visits, and for a time-poor traveller it is the only version of this corridor that includes the temples and the guide.

What you see at each temple

Esna, the Temple of Khnum. Only the hypostyle hall survives, dating to the Roman period under Tiberius, and it sits in a pit below modern street level. Conservators from Egypt's Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities and the University of Tübingen have spent years cleaning it: the ceiling work was finished in 2023 and work on the walls continues. The painted columns and astronomical ceiling are a detail most visitors miss. The foreign adult ticket is EGP 200.

Edfu, the Temple of Horus. Building began in 237 BC under Ptolemy III and finished in 57 BC; buried in sand for centuries afterwards, it survives remarkably intact, and it is one of the best-preserved temples in Egypt. Walls of hieroglyphs and a hypostyle hall, a forest of stone columns, reward the time you spend here. The foreign adult ticket is EGP 550.

Kom Ombo, the double temple. Dedicated to two gods, Sobek, the crocodile god, and Haroeris, Horus the Elder, with everything duplicated: twin entrances, halls and sanctuaries side by side. It sits on the river bank, and a small museum next door displays mummified crocodiles, with its own ticket. The foreign adult ticket is EGP 450.

The three temple tickets come to EGP 1,200 for a foreign adult, about €20 at EGP 60 to the euro (8 November 2026). On the €67 southbound day they are included; on the downriver day, budget for them.

Going the other way: Aswan to Luxor by road

If you have done Aswan, with Philae, the High Dam and perhaps Abu Simbel, and Luxor is next, the downriver day turns the transfer into the sightseeing. It leaves Aswan with a hotel pickup and visits the temples in the order the Nile flows: Kom Ombo first, while the air is still cool, then Edfu, the longest visit, then Esna, a short stop in the town, before a hotel drop-off in Luxor in the late afternoon. Allow for a lunch stop on top of the driving.

It is a one-way day, so book a Luxor bed for that night. It suits anyone flying or taking the train out of Luxor the next morning, and anyone who arrived in Aswan by cruise and wants the temples the cruise did not include. A northbound cruise such as Nile Discovery also calls at Kom Ombo and Edfu, but not Esna; if your Luxor nights are already booked, take the road day and spend the cruise money on Luxor's tombs and temples instead.

How to choose in four questions

Four questions, in order, and the corridor picks its own option:

  1. How many days can this leg have? Four or five: the cruise. One: the Temple Road or the train.
  2. Do you want a guide? Yes: cruise or Temple Road. No: train or private car.
  3. How many of you are there? Four or more: ask for a private-car quote and compare it per person with the Temple Road. The crossover is real.
  4. Is the journey part of the experience? If the river itself is the point, nothing replaces the cruise. If the temples are the point, the Temple Road collects them in a day the train wastes.

A pattern many itineraries use: cruise one direction, road the other, so the temples never repeat. Nile Discovery (Aswan to Luxor) paired with a southbound Temple Road day is exactly that shape. Each is a separate departure, so book flights only after each date confirms.

Safety and checkpoints on the road

Expect routine checkpoints along the Nile Valley road and carry your passport rather than a copy; the FCDO says police check ID regularly (27 October 2026). A road day that ends in the afternoon keeps you inside the FCDO's advice against driving outside main cities at night. If you drive yourself, Earth Trekkers recommend hiring a driver instead.

Most travellers need an Egyptian visa; check the current rules and fee on the official Egypt e-visa portal before you fly.

How booking works on Sawa

Sawa runs a fixed catalogue of shared departures and sets the calendar and the prices. Each date is operated by one of the licensed Egyptian agencies with travellers on the date, named before the deposit is due. Reserving a seat is free, with no card, and nothing is charged before the GoAhead, the moment four travellers (people, not bookings) have reserved the date.

On the road days, a 10% deposit is paid by payment link at the GoAhead, and the balance is due 2 days (48 hours) before departure. A forming date has until seven days before the tour to reach four; if it does not, it is cancelled, nothing is charged and another date is suggested. Cancelling at least 48 hours before departure is a full refund; under 48 hours you lose the 10% deposit; force majeure is a full refund. A traveller who does not pay after the GoAhead is excluded and the tour still runs; a confirmed date is not cancelled for low numbers. The price is fixed per traveller, with no solo surcharge on day tours, and when a departure fills, a new independent departure opens.

The cruises follow the package terms: a 25% deposit, the balance 14 days before, and cancellation free 30 or more days before, half the deposit (12.5%) from 29 to 15 days, and the full deposit (25%) at 14 days or fewer. Some components may become non-refundable earlier, and this is disclosed before payment. On cruises, solo cabins are confirmed in the booking, with no promise in advance.

Payment is by a secure payment link from Online Era (General Sales Agent licence 32241); charges are in euros. The full steps are in how the GoAhead works and the terms.

The short version

Luxor and Aswan sit about 215 to 245 km apart, and the four ways between them trade time against temples: the train is cheapest and empty, the private car is flexible and unguided, the cruise is everything at the cost of days (from €500 or €610), and the Temple Road is the river temples in one guided day, from €54, €60 or €67 depending on direction and stops (as listed in November 2026). Time-rich: sail. Time-poor: take the Temple Road. faq.q: What is the best way to get from Luxor to Aswan?
faq.a: It depends on your days: the train for cheap point-to-point, a private car for flexibility, a Nile cruise if you have four or five days, and the guided Temple Road if you have one day and want Esna, Edfu and Kom Ombo included. For time-poor travellers, the Temple Road is the option that turns the transfer into the sightseeing.

faq.q: How far is Luxor from Aswan?
faq.a: About 215 km on the direct road, or about 245 km on the riverside route through the temple towns. That is roughly three hours by car without stops, about three and a half by train, and four or five days by cruise boat.

faq.q: Is there a train from Luxor to Aswan?
faq.a: Yes. Foreigner fares for 2026 run from about US$26 to US$77 one way depending on train and class (Seat 61), and the journey takes about three and a half hours. Foreigners buy at the tourist window at the station or through an agency, because the national railway's website and app sell to Egyptians only. It is transport, not sightseeing: it does not stop at the temples.

faq.q: Can you visit Esna, Edfu and Kom Ombo in one day?
faq.a: Yes, in either direction. The southbound day from Luxor (from €67, tickets and lunch included) and the downriver day from Aswan (from €60, temple tickets and lunch included) each take about eight hours with a licensed guide. Doing it yourself by car is possible, but you carry the guiding and the timing yourself.

faq.q: Can I do the trip from Aswan to Luxor instead?
faq.a: Yes. The downriver day leaves Aswan, visits Kom Ombo, Edfu and Esna in that order, and drops you at your Luxor hotel in the late afternoon. Choose whichever direction matches your flights and your cruise.

faq.q: Is the Nile cruise worth it over the road?
faq.a: If you have four or five days and want the river itself as the experience, yes: the cruise is the classic for a reason. If your itinerary is tight, the Temple Road puts the corridor's temples into one guided day and hands the saved days to Luxor, Aswan or Abu Simbel.

faq.q: Do I need to worry about checkpoints on the road?
faq.a: Expect routine checkpoints and carry your passport. They are a normal part of driving in the Nile Valley.
